problem_statement:
*** Problem Statement ***

Consider a $2025\times2025$ grid of unit squares. Matilda wishes to place on the grid some rectangular tiles, possibly of difference sizes, such that each side of every tile lies on a grid line and every unit square is covered by at most one tile.

Determine the minimum number of tiles Matilda needs to place so that each row and each column of the grid has exactly one unit square that is not covered by any tile.
solution:
Summary**

**a. Verdict:** I have found a complete solution. The minimum possible number of tiles is  

\[
\boxed{4048}.
\]

**b. Method Sketch**

1. **Permutation of uncovered squares.**  
   Because each row and each column must contain exactly one uncovered unit square, the uncovered squares form a permutation matrix: there is a permutation \(p\) of \(\{1,\dots ,n\}\) (\(n=2025\)) such that the uncovered square in row \(i\) is \((i,p(i))\).

2. **Two disjoint regions.**  
   For each row \(i\) define  
   \[
   L_i=\{(i,j)\mid 1\le j<p(i)\},\qquad 
   R_i=\{(i,j)\mid p(i)<j\le n\}.
   \]
   The set of all covered squares is the disjoint union \(L\cup R\) where \(L=\bigcup_iL_i\) (the “left” part) and \(R=\bigcup_iR_i\) (the “right” part).

3. **Lower bound for each part.**  
   *Lemma 1.* In \(L\) each row \(i\) with \(p(i)>1\) has a **rightmost** cell \(r_i=(i,p(i)-1)\). Any axis‑parallel rectangle contained in \(L\) can contain at most one such cell.  
   *Proof.* Let a rectangle be \(I\times J\) with \(J=[a,c]\) (so \(c\) is its rightmost column). Since the rectangle lies in \(L\), for every row \(i\in I\) we have \(p(i)>c\); hence \(p(i)-1\ge c\). The cell \(r_i\) lies in column \(p(i)-1\), so it belongs to the rectangle only when \(p(i)-1=c\). Because the numbers \(p(i)-1\) are all distinct, at most one row satisfies this, proving the claim. ∎  

   There are exactly \(n-1\) rightmost cells (all rows except the one with \(p(i)=1\)). Consequently any tiling of \(L\) needs at least \(n-1\) rectangles. An identical argument applied to the **leftmost** cells \(\ell_i=(i,p(i)+1)\) of the right part \(R\) yields the same bound for \(R\). Hence any tiling of the whole board uses at least  

   \[
   (n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2
   \tag{1}
   \]

   tiles.

4. **Construction attaining the bound.**  
   For each row \(i\) place the following horizontal tiles:

   * If \(p(i)>1\), place a tile covering the whole left segment of the row,
     \[
     T_i^{L}= \{(i,j)\mid 1\le j<p(i)\}.
     \]
   * If \(p(i)<n\), place a tile covering the whole right segment of the row,
     \[
     T_i^{R}= \{(i,j)\mid p(i)<j\le n\}.
     \]

   Each \(T_i^{L}\) (resp. \(T_i^{R}\)) is a rectangle of height 1 and width \(p(i)-1\) (resp. \(n-p(i)\).)  
   The left and right tiles of a given row are separated by the uncovered square \((i,p(i))\); tiles belonging to different rows lie in different rows, so all tiles are pairwise disjoint and together cover exactly \(L\cup R\).  

   Counting tiles: exactly one row has \(p(i)=1\) (no left tile) and exactly one row has \(p(i)=n\) (no right tile). Hence the total number of tiles is  

   \[
   \bigl|\{i\mid p(i)>1\}\bigr|+\bigl|\{i\mid p(i)<n\}\bigr|
   =(n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2 .
   \tag{2}
   \]

5. **Conclusion.**  
   The lower bound (1) and the explicit construction (2) coincide, so the minimum possible number of tiles is \(2n-2\). For \(n=2025\) this equals  

   \[
   2\cdot2025-2=4048 .
   \]

   Hence the answer is \(\boxed{4048}\).

---

**Detailed Solution**

Let \(n=2025\).  Denote the set of unit squares of the board by  

\[
B=\{(i,j)\mid 1\le i,j\le n\},
\]

where the first coordinate is the row index and the second the column index.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  The uncovered squares form a permutation matrix

Since each row and each column must contain exactly one uncovered unit square,
there exists a permutation \(p\) of \(\{1,\dots ,n\}\) such that the uncovered
square in row \(i\) is \((i,p(i))\).  Thus the set of uncovered squares is  

\[
U=\{(i,p(i))\mid i=1,\dots ,n\}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Left and right regions

For each row \(i\) define  

\[
L_i=\{(i,j)\mid 1\le j<p(i)\},\qquad 
R_i=\{(i,j)\mid p(i)<j\le n\}.
\]

The squares that must be covered are  

\[
C=B\setminus U = L\cup R,\qquad 
L=\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}L_i,\; R=\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}R_i .
\]

The two sets \(L\) and \(R\) are disjoint, because a square cannot be simultaneously
to the left and to the right of the same uncovered square.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  A lower bound for the left part \(L\)

For every row \(i\) with \(p(i)>1\) let  

\[
r_i=(i,p(i)-1)
\]

be the **rightmost** cell of that row inside \(L\).  There are exactly
\(n-1\) such cells (all rows except the unique row with \(p(i)=1\)).

---

#### Lemma 1  
Any axis‑parallel rectangle contained in \(L\) contains at most one
rightmost cell \(r_i\).

*Proof.*  
Let a rectangle be \(R=I\times J\) where \(I\) is a set of consecutive rows
and \(J=[a,c]\) a set of consecutive columns; thus \(c\) is the rightmost
column of the rectangle.  Because \(R\subseteq L\), for every row \(i\in I\)
we must have \(p(i)>c\); otherwise the square \((i,c)\) would lie outside
\(L\).  Hence \(p(i)-1\ge c\) for all \(i\in I\).

The rightmost cell of row \(i\) is \(r_i=(i,p(i)-1)\), which lies in column
\(p(i)-1\).  For \(r_i\) to belong to the rectangle we need
\(p(i)-1\le c\).  Combining with the inequality \(p(i)-1\ge c\) we obtain
\(p(i)-1=c\).  Thus a rectangle can contain a rightmost cell only from a row
with \(p(i)-1=c\).  Since the numbers \(p(i)-1\) are all distinct, at most
one row satisfies this condition.  ∎

---

Because each of the \(n-1\) rightmost cells must be covered, Lemma 1 implies
that any tiling of \(L\) uses at least \(n-1\) rectangles:

\[
f(L)\ge n-1. \tag{3}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  A lower bound for the right part \(R\)

For every row \(i\) with \(p(i)<n\) define the **leftmost** cell of the
right part  

\[
\ell_i=(i,p(i)+1).
\]

Exactly \(n-1\) such cells exist (all rows except the one with \(p(i)=n\)).
An argument symmetric to Lemma 1 shows that any rectangle contained in \(R\)
contains at most one \(\ell_i\).  Consequently

\[
f(R)\ge n-1. \tag{4}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Global lower bound

Since the two parts are disjoint, any tiling of the whole set \(C\) needs at
least  

\[
f(L)+f(R)\ge (n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2 \tag{5}
\]

tiles.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6.  Construction achieving the bound

For each row \(i\) we place the following horizontal tiles:

* **Left tile.** If \(p(i)>1\) let  

  \[
  T_i^{L}= \{(i,j)\mid 1\le j<p(i)\}.
  \]

  This is a rectangle of height 1 and width \(p(i)-1\).

* **Right tile.** If \(p(i)<n\) let  

  \[
  T_i^{R}= \{(i,j)\mid p(i)<j\le n\}.
  \]

  This is a rectangle of height 1 and width \(n-p(i)\).

The left and right tiles of the same row are separated by the uncovered
square \((i,p(i))\); tiles belonging to different rows lie in different rows,
hence all tiles are pairwise disjoint.  Together they cover precisely the
sets \(L\) and \(R\).

Counting tiles: exactly one row has \(p(i)=1\) (no left tile) and exactly one
row has \(p(i)=n\) (no right tile).  Therefore the total number of tiles is  

\[
\bigl|\{i\mid p(i)>1\}\bigr|+\bigl|\{i\mid p(i)<n\}\bigr|
=(n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2 .
\tag{6}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 7.  Conclusion

The lower bound (5) and the explicit tiling (6) coincide.  Hence the minimum
possible number of tiles is  

\[
2n-2 = 2\cdot2025-2 = 4048 .
\]

\[
\boxed{4048}
\]

* The construction uses only horizontal rectangles of height 1, which are
  legitimate tiles; each tile is explicitly described and shown to be disjoint.
* The counting of tiles is exact, giving the final answer \(\boxed{4048}\).
